capabilities.title: PostgreSQL repository implementation
capabilities.notes: Real driver, real database, real transactions. Inventory found scripts/run-migrations.js to be a single console.log and the only test of the SQL to read the files as text and grep for CREATE TABLE, so twenty migrations had never been executed anywhere. They do apply to vanilla PostgreSQL 16 - only pgcrypto and current_setting('app.*') session variables, nothing Supabase-specific - but they cannot back the repository contract: user_identities requires tenant_neutral_subject_id and primary_authentication_method that no engine sets, and audit_records types aggregate_id as UUID while PermissionService audits a permission key there, an insert that would fail in production. A forward migration adds a schema shaped like the contract and leaves all twenty untouched. Driver is postgres.js: one package, no transitive dependencies, tagged templates so parameterization is the default and sql.unsafe is the single statically policeable escape hatch. Entities whose invariants CLAUDE.md depends on have their own tables with real foreign keys and partial unique indexes; history is append-only in the database through a trigger, and a check constraint makes a severed chain link unstorable rather than merely detectable. Two defects surfaced: the audit integrity hash was not canonical, hashing the calling engine's object literal so no store rebuilding a record from columns could reproduce it, and a session-scoped advisory lock cannot guard a migration run behind a pool. Evidence is 66 tests against a live instance covering conformance, restart durability across two pools, transaction rollback with mutation and audit coupled, isolation, one-winner concurrency, a fork-free chain under twelve concurrent writers, and tamper detection. The gate fails rather than skips without ASSURAPAY_TEST_DATABASE_URL. Row Level Security remains persistence.rls-certification: the policies exist on the historical tables but are not certified, and the trust-store tables do not yet carry them.

capabilities.title: Production persistence runtime wiring
capabilities.notes: apps/web/lib/trust-app.ts constructed an InMemoryTrustStore on globalThis - a production composition root choosing volatile storage in one line that reads as caching. Every grant, membership and audit record the deployed application wrote was lost when the process recycled, while the application kept answering and authorization kept deciding. Persistence is now selected once by createPersistenceRuntime from validated server-only configuration that refuses the memory adapter for every durable deployment class, refuses a missing database URL with no localhost fallback, requires TLS to be stated explicitly, and rejects any NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable that could influence it. There is no fallback anywhere: an unreachable database fails startup or reports unready, and never substitutes a store. Readiness is more than connectivity - a reachable database with no tables, or a required migration unapplied, is not ready - and is checked live rather than cached, so a probe cannot report healthy through an outage. Liveness is separate and does no I/O, so an orchestrator does not restart a healthy process because its database blinked. The readiness gate is applied inside authorizedContextForRoute, which every protected route already passes through, rather than in 161 handlers that would each have to remember it. One production host exists (the Next.js app); no worker, scheduler, consumer, webhook or outbox dispatcher exists in the repository, so none was migrated and none was invented. FileAssuraStore is left alone: it implements AssuraRepository, a separate bounded context covering engine 06-60 domain state, writes a JSON file, and seeds demo data - a legacy production store needing retirement, which is its own capability rather than a side effect of this one. Certified against a real database through the production path only, never by constructing PostgresTrustStore directly.

capabilities.title: Row Level Security certification
capabilities.notes: The defect was found against a live instance rather than by reading SQL. One hundred tables already carried ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and a policy requiring workspace_id = current_workspace_id(), and none of it applied to the application: ENABLE does not constrain a table's owner, and the application role owned every table. Inserting a membership, clearing app.workspace_id and counting rows returned one, on a table whose policy said zero. A policy present but bypassed is worse than none because it is read as protection. Corrected by FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on every governed trust table, so the owner is subject to its own policies, plus a non-owning assurapay_app role holding DML only - and no DELETE on history, so a role that cannot issue the statement cannot reach the trigger that would refuse it. Scope reaches the database through transaction-local session variables set by the repository from an AsyncLocalStorage the composition root establishes: TrustPersistence takes no context, and adding one would change every method and call site a second time. Transaction-local because a global set_config would leave one request's tenant on the pooled connection for the next, which is a cross-tenant read with no bug in any policy. An unscoped operation reads nothing rather than everything - the honest failure mode of ambient scope, and why scope is established at the funnel every protected route passes through. Certification is never 'does a policy exist': it checks enabled, forced, and policy-present, then runs live denial probes as the non-owning role for cross-tenant read, cross-tenant write through WITH CHECK, and the unscoped case. Named weak point: trust_records rows with neither tenant nor workspace - identities and sessions, which exist before any workspace and are how a caller establishes who they are - are visible to any scoped caller and still depend on application-level scoping. Narrowing that needs a tenant column on those records, which is a data-model change rather than a policy one. The 20 historical engine tables remain ENABLE-only and uncertified; this capability covers the trust store.

capabilities.title: Route-level permission mapping
capabilities.notes: Declares the authorization policy for the whole HTTP surface as a route table keyed on template|METHOD, resolves a requirement from a live request path and method, and applies it at the composition root through authorizedContextForRoute. Fails closed: an unmapped route or method throws rather than defaulting to allow. This capability is the policy and the enforcement entry point, not the per-route migration — see trust.permission-grant-catalogue and trust.route-permission-rollout, which cannot precede it.

capabilities.title: Permission grant catalogue and workspace bootstrap
capabilities.notes: Closes the circle that blocked the route migration: deny-by-default over an empty grant table denies everyone, including whoever would issue the first grant. PERMISSION_CATALOGUE is the closed set of roles and the keys each may hold, so a key no role names cannot be granted. SEGREGATION_CATALOGUE is the canonical duty pairs, mirrored by the route table and kept in step by a test. bootstrapWorkspaceGrants grants the founding administrator with no authorizing caller, once per workspace, against an owner membership that must already exist. grantRole is the ordinary authorized path and refuses a grant whose resulting permission set would breach segregation of duties. No superuser role exists: the founding administrator holds no certification, release or payment key, so founding a workspace does not create a principal who can move money alone.

capabilities.title: Route migration to authorized context
capabilities.notes: All 154 non-public route handlers call authorizedContextForRoute; no handler calls requestContext. A source-scanning coverage suite fails certification if a route skips authorization, if the policy table and the filesystem disagree in either direction, or if a handler reads actor, workspace or tenant from the request body. Eight legacy routes additionally had no authentication at all and took tenantId, workspaceId and actorId from the body with demo defaults; those now derive all three from the authorized context. The allowlist is three auth routes, each with a stated reason.

capabilities.title: Identity assertion issuance from an authenticated session
capabilities.notes: Joins sign-in to the authorized API. Deliberately not IdentityGateway.exchange, which stays unsupported: exchange transfers privilege between assertions under ungoverned attenuation rules, whereas issuance starts from a session the identity engine owns and can revoke, and mints something strictly weaker. Four rules make that true - every claim is copied from the stored session so no request field can name a subject or raise assurance; the assertion expires at the lesser of the configured TTL and the session remaining, so revocation cannot be outlasted; a workspace may be selected only from ACTIVE memberships; and the session-to-assertion binding is audited as its own event, keyed on the session, distinct from the gateway record keyed on the nonce.

capabilities.title: HTTP surface for workspace founding and role assignment
capabilities.notes: Three routes make the authorization model operable: found a workspace, read the role catalogue, assign a role. Founding is identity-class because it creates the first grant and requiring a permission would restore the deadlock; it is safe because bootstrapWorkspaceGrants refuses unless the caller is already an ACTIVE OWNER and the workspace holds no grant. The founder is the authenticated caller and the assignment workspace is the caller active one, so neither can be named from the request. No route grants a permission key directly - grants are made by assigning a catalogue role, which is what applies the segregation-of-duties check.

capabilities.title: TrustPersistence conformance specification
capabilities.notes: Every engine reads and writes through TrustPersistence and the audit hash chain is computed inside it, yet nothing tested it directly - the behaviour the platform depends on was whatever the single implementation happened to do. The suite states that behaviour as framework-free checks a Postgres adapter runs by importing the same module, so both stores are held to one standard rather than two descriptions of the same intent. Writing it immediately found a defect: list() shallow-copied, handing out live references to stored records, so any caller could edit auditRecords in place with no write call.

capabilities.title: Asynchronous repository interface
capabilities.notes: The real blocker on the Postgres adapter, fixed with no infrastructure. TrustPersistence was synchronous in every method - list returned T[], append returned void - so no network-backed store could implement it, and CLAUDE.md's claim that Postgres can be swapped without touching engine logic was false as built. The interface itself was made asynchronous rather than adding a parallel AsyncTrustPersistence: two interfaces would let call sites keep the synchronous one, and a MaybePromise union would let a caller forget to await and still compile. Evidence is the static enforcement rather than the type declaration, because TrustPersistence existed before this capability and a symbol probe on it would have reported the work as done before it started. Every forbidden shape typechecks, so the rules in packages/reos/src/validators/persistence.ts are what keeps the migration from eroding: floating governed writes, void-discarded writes, async predicates handed to synchronous array methods, a pre-awaited Promise.race, and a sync method back on the interface. Each rule corresponds to a defect the migration actually produced: ValidationAcceptanceTestingEngine.passed used every(async) and so passed unconditionally, IdentityService.revokeAll returned unresolved promises, and the AI gateway awaited its provider inside the race that was supposed to time it out.

capabilities.title: Trust schema ownership reconciliation
capabilities.notes: Every trust aggregate had two relational models and no declared owner. The certified PostgresTrustStore writes ten trust_* tables; an earlier thirty-one-table model described the same aggregates, was created by every migration run, and typed audit_records.aggregate_id as UUID while the live store audits permission keys. Two facts established against a live instance decided the scope. There were never any dual writes: the only production module issuing SQL against data is postgres-store.ts and it names trust_* tables only, FileAssuraStore contains no SQL at all, and every historical table name outside supabase/migrations appears in a test - so the historical model held no rows and this is a retirement, not a data migration. Reporting migrated-row counts would have been fabrication. And the model is not uniformly removable: PostgreSQL was the oracle rather than inference, refusing the drop and naming governed_executions_workspace_id_fkey, which fixes the surviving closure at workspaces (foreign-key parent of 93 Engine 06-60 tables), workspace_memberships (read by has_active_workspace_membership(), called by those tables' policies) and user_identities (parent of workspace_memberships). Those three are retained as compatibility objects with persistence.domain-store-durability as a named retirement condition, not an indefinite reprieve; the other twenty-eight are dropped by forward migration that re-checks emptiness at apply time and refuses rather than discarding, because 'these tables are empty' is a claim about every database that will ever apply it. Readiness distinguishes certified from safe-to-serve: two models for one aggregate or a runtime that can write what it does not own blocks startup, while a retained object that has since been dropped is registry staleness and must not. Scope is the trust domain only - Engine 06-60 domain state remains FileAssuraStore-backed and its durability is not claimed.

capabilities.title: Asynchronous domain repository interface
capabilities.notes: The real blocker on the Engine 06-60 Postgres adapter, and the exact defect persistence.async-repository-interface fixed for the trust domain one year of capabilities earlier. AssuraRepository declared getSnapshot(): Snapshot and setSnapshot(...): void - synchronous, across 115 production and test call sites, none awaited. No network-backed store can implement either, because JavaScript cannot block on I/O: the only way to satisfy the old signature was to hold the whole database in memory and return the cache, which is arrays behind a PostgreSQL adapter rather than durability and is explicitly forbidden. So persistence.domain-store-durability was unimplementable rather than merely unstarted, and this is its prerequisite. The interface itself was made asynchronous rather than adding a parallel async variant, for the same reasons recorded against the trust capability: two interfaces let call sites keep the synchronous one, and a MaybePromise union lets a caller forget to await and still compile. A second defect surfaced while fixing the first - getSnapshot returned this.snapshot, so every caller held a live handle to the store's interior and could mutate persisted state with no write method, no validation and nothing in the audit trail to attribute it to. normalizeSnapshot was not sufficient as a defence because it builds a new outer object while reusing the same arrays; the store now detaches on both read and write. Enforcement was generalised: the sync-interface-method rule checked TrustPersistence only, which is how the second contract stayed synchronous while the first was certified. Not claimed: no PostgreSQL domain store, no domain schema, no JSON migration, no domain RLS, no cutover. getSnapshot remains snapshot-shaped, so a relational implementation would read every collection per call - implementable and durable, but an efficiency problem persistence.domain-store-durability must address by moving to per-collection reads.

capabilities.title: Domain store durability for Engines 06-60
capabilities.notes: Selected, not started. FileAssuraStore remains production-active for Engines 06-60: it is JSON files with demo seeding, implements a different contract from TrustPersistence, is not covered by PostgreSQL row-level security, and is what prevents any platform-wide durability claim. Schema ownership reconciliation deliberately did not touch it - the trust domain now has one canonical relational owner per aggregate, and the ninety-five Engine 06-60 tables are classified OUT_OF_SCOPE_DOMAIN rather than claimed, because claiming ownership of a model nothing reads or writes would assert durability that does not exist. Two concrete inheritances from that capability define the starting point. First, one hundred and two of those tables carry ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY with no FORCE - the same defect persistence.rls-certification corrected for the trust tables - so a boundary that reads as protection enforces nothing on them. Second, three trust-domain tables (workspaces, workspace_memberships, user_identities) could not be retired because that model depends on them, and this capability is their named retirement condition: it must decide whether Engine 06-60 state becomes relational at all, and if so what parents its workspace foreign keys.
